tip: 'Manquer à' is reversed from English: 'Mon pays me manque' = My country is missing to me = I miss my country. The thing missed is subject.
'Cet' is used before masculine nouns starting with a vowel or silent 'h': 'cet homme', 'cet arbre', 'cet hôtel'.
'Bonjour' is used from morning to evening. Use 'bonsoir' after around 6 pm.
'À tout à l'heure' = see you later (today). 'À plus tard' = see you later (less specific). 'À bientôt' = see you soon.
Weather uses 'il fait' + adjective: 'il fait beau' (nice), 'il fait chaud' (hot), 'il fait froid' (cold), 'il fait mauvais' (bad).
You don't 'need' something in French, you 'have need of' it: 'avoir besoin de'. 'J'ai besoin de me reposer' is literally 'I have need of resting.' The 'de' is not optional.
'Sur place' literally means 'on the spot' and is how you say eating in, not takeaway. At a café you'll hear 'sur place ou à emporter?' = for here or to go?
'Plaire à' has a reverse construction: the thing liked is the subject. 'Ce film me plaît' = This movie pleases me (= I like this movie).
The easiest question needs no extra words: keep normal order and raise your voice. 'Ça te plaît ici ?' is a statement asked with a rising tone.
'Vous' here is formal singular. French normally uses 'vous' with strangers and superiors.
You have your age in French: 'mon fils a trois ans' is literally 'my son has three years'. Use 'avoir', not 'être', for age.
'Avoir hâte de' = to look forward to, literally 'to have haste to.' 'J'ai hâte de te revoir' = I can't wait to see you again. The impatience is a thing you possess, not a feeling.
'Je voudrais' is the polite way to say 'I would like', softer than 'je veux' (I want). Both are forms of 'vouloir' (to want).
'Il me semble que' = it seems to me that. 'Sembler' takes the person as 'me' or 'te': 'il me semble', 'il te semble'.
French floors: 'rez-de-chaussée' (ground floor), 'premier étage' (1st floor = US 2nd floor), 'deuxième étage' (2nd = US 3rd).
'Mettre' can express duration: 'j'ai mis' + time means it took me + time.
'Aux yeux bleus' = with blue eyes. 'Aux' is the contraction of 'à les'. Used for physical descriptions.
The feminine '-e' makes the silent letter heard: masculine 'brun' ends silently, but 'brune' sounds the 'n'.
'Le dimanche' with the article means every Sunday, not one particular one: 'Nous dînons en famille le dimanche' = we have dinner as a family on Sundays. Drop the 'le' for a single Sunday.
Quantity words normally take plain 'de', not 'du' or 'de la': 'assez d'eau' = enough water. Same for 'beaucoup d'eau', 'trop d'eau'.
In a command the pronoun moves behind the verb and 'te' turns into 'toi': 'Dépêche-toi' = hurry up. Compare the plain statement 'tu te dépêches'.
'Ça te dit de...' = do you feel like...? Literally 'does that say to you to...'. The idea is the subject, not you.
'De' marks which train by its time: 'le train de huit heures' = the eight o'clock train. It's 'the train of eight hours'.
'Personne' means nobody, but it still needs 'ne' before the verb – and no 'pas': 'personne ne connaissait' = nobody knew.
'Aussitôt dit, aussitôt fait' is literally 'as soon as said, as soon as done' – the French for 'no sooner said than done.'
'Le monde' means 'people' here, not 'the world': 'tellement de monde' = so many people. It stays singular, so the verb is 'est venu'.
'Déplaire à' is the opposite of 'plaire à': 'ça me déplaît' = I don't like that. The thing disliked is the subject.
You play an instrument with 'jouer de', not plain 'jouer'. 'Jouer du piano' packs 'de' + 'le' into 'du' = to play the piano. Sports flip to 'jouer à': 'jouer au foot'.
'S'il vous plaît' (formal/plural) vs 's'il te plaît' (informal). Literally 'if it pleases you'. Essential polite expression.
After a negative, French usually swaps the article for 'de': not 'un problème' but 'pas de problème'. Same with 'je n'ai pas de temps'.
